title: Valid Anagram
description: You are given two strings, s and t. Your job is to check if t is an anagram of s. anagrams:- Two strings are anagrams of each other if they contain the exact same letters the exact same number of times, just in a different order.

examples.explanation: Both strings use the exact same letters the exact same number of times, just in a different order.
'rat' has an 'r' and a 't', but 'car' has a 'c' instead — the letters don't match.

constraints: s and t consist of lowercase English letters
hints: If the two strings have different lengths, you can immediately return false — no need to check further.
A simple 26-slot counting array (one slot per letter a-z) works great and is faster than a hash map here.
relatedProblems: Find All Anagrams in a String
followUp: What changes if the inputs contain Unicode characters instead of just lowercase letters?

testCases.note: Basic case — same letters, different order.
Different letters entirely.
Edge case: smallest possible input, single matching letter.
Edge case: different lengths — can never be anagrams.
Edge case: repeated letters, still matches when counted correctly.

title: Valid Palindrome
description: Given a string s, determine whether it is a palindrome after considering only alphanumeric characters and ignoring letter case. A palindrome is a string that reads the same forward and backward. Return true if the string is a palindrome; otherwise, return false.

examples.input: s = "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"
examples.explanation: After removing punctuation/spaces and lowercasing, it becomes 'amanaplanacanalpanama', which reads the same both ways.
After cleaning it becomes 'raceacar', which is not the same backwards.

constraints: s consists only of printable ASCII characters
hints: You don't need to build a new cleaned string — just skip invalid characters as you move the two pointers.
Convert letters to lowercase using simple math on their character codes instead of a slow library function in a loop.
followUp: Can you solve Valid Palindrome II, where exactly one deletion is allowed?

testCases.input: s = "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"
testCases.note: Classic case with spaces, commas, and mixed case.
Not a palindrome once cleaned.
Edge case: single character is always a palindrome.
Edge case: string with only punctuation becomes empty after cleaning — an empty string counts as a valid palindrome.
Edge case: mix of a digit and a letter that don't match each other.

title: Reverse String
description: You're given an array of characters, s. Your job is to reverse the order of the characters — but you must do it 'in-place', meaning you edit the same array directly instead of creating a brand-new reversed array.

examples.explanation: Swap the first and last letters, then the second and second-to-last, and so on.
Same swapping approach works for any length, even length included.

constraints: s[i] is a printable ASCII character
hints: You must modify the input array directly, using no extra array of significant size.
Stop the pointers once left is greater than or equal to right, so it works for both even and odd lengths.

testCases.note: Standard odd-length example.

Edge case: already a palindrome, output looks unchanged.
Edge case: repeated characters still swap positionally.

title: Longest Common Prefix
description: You're given a list of strings. Find the longest starting piece of text (called a 'prefix') that every single string in the list begins with. If the strings don't share any common starting letters at all, return an empty string.

examples.explanation: All three words start with 'f' and 'l', but then they differ.
The very first letters ('d', 'r', 'c') don't even match, so there's no common prefix at all.

hints: Use the first string as your starting guess for the prefix, then shrink it down as you compare against the rest.
If your candidate prefix ever becomes empty, you can stop early and just return an empty string.

title: Find the Index of the First Occurrence in a String

Edge case: overlapping repeated characters — match found at the earliest valid position.

title: Detect Capital
description: You're given a single word. Check if its use of capital letters follows one of these three allowed patterns:,
every single letter is uppercase (like 'USA')

title: String to Integer (atoi)
description: You need to build a mini version of the 'atoi' function: convert a string into a proper 32-bit integer, following these exact steps in order — skip any leading spaces, then look for an optional '+' or '-' sign, then read as many digits as you can find in a row, and ignore anything that comes after those digits. If the resulting number is too big or too small to fit in a 32-bit integer, clamp it to the maximum or minimum allowed value instead.

title: Group Anagrams
description: You're given a list of strings. Group all the strings that are anagrams of each other into their own separate lists.

title: Decode Ways
description: Imagine a code where 'A' maps to '1', 'B' maps to '2', all the way up to 'Z' mapping to '26'. You're given a string made only of digits, and you need to count how many different ways it could have been decoded back into letters using this mapping. At each position in the string, you have up to two choices: decode the current single digit alone (as long as it's not '0', since there's no letter for that), or combine it with the digit right before it into a two-digit number (as long as that two-digit number is between 10 and 26). You add up the number of ways from each valid choice.

examples.explanation: It can be decoded as 'AB' (1, 2) or as 'L' (12) — two possible ways.
It can become 'BZ' (2, 26), 'VF' (22, 6), or 'BBF' (2, 2, 6).

constraints: s consists only of digits and may contain leading zeros
hints: A '0' can never be decoded by itself — any branch that tries this is automatically invalid.
You can use just two rolling variables instead of a full array to keep track of previous results, saving memory.
expectedSpaceComplexity: O(1) with rolling variables, O(n) with a full DP array
followUp: What changes if a '*' wildcard digit could represent any value from 1-9, as in Decode Ways II?

testCases.note: Two valid ways to decode.

Edge case: a lone '0' can never be decoded — no valid ways.
Edge case: leading zero makes the two-digit combination invalid too.
Edge case: '0' can't stand alone, so it must combine with the '1' before it — only one valid way.

title: Generate Parentheses

description: You're given two version numbers written like '1.2' or '1.10'. title: Regular Expression Matching

title: Wildcard Matching
description: You need to build a pattern matcher that supports '?' It's similar to Regular Expression Matching, but '*' behaves differently here — it doesn't depend on the character before it, it can swallow any run of characters on its own.

For the faster two-pointer version, remember the last position of a '*' you've seen so you can backtrack and try a wider match whenever there's a mismatch.
